questions.q: If you already know Azure Monitor from Azure Fundamentals, what is actually new in this lesson?
options: Applying the same platform-wide service specifically to a SQL database's own metrics — the service itself doesn't change
Azure Monitor is a completely different, SQL-only product from what Azure Fundamentals covered
Azure SQL databases require a separate paid monitoring agent that other Azure resources don't need
Azure Monitor cannot be used with Azure SQL Database at all
questions.explain: Azure Monitor is the same collection and alerting service behind every Azure resource; this lesson applies it to the specific signals a SQL database emits.

questions.q: Which of these is a metric Azure SQL emits automatically that a DBA watches day to day, per this lesson?
options: connection_failed — a spike often shows a problem before query performance does
lines_of_tsql_written — how much SQL code developers wrote that day
number_of_indexes_created_this_year
average_employee_satisfaction_score
questions.explain: connection_successful/connection_failed, DTU or CPU percent, storage percent, and deadlock count are the core metrics called out in this lesson.

questions.q: What are the three required parts of an Azure Monitor alert rule, in the order this lesson presents them?
options: Signal (the metric), Condition (threshold + window), and Action group (what happens when it fires)
Username, password, and connection string
Database name, table name, and column name
Only a threshold — nothing else is required
questions.explain: Skip the action group specifically and the alert condition still fires, but silently — nothing actually notifies anyone.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what does a fired alert (e.g. "DTU crossed 90%") actually tell you, and what does it NOT tell you?
options: It tells you that the threshold was crossed; it does not tell you which query, which session, or why — that's a separate investigation step
It tells you exactly which query and session caused it, with no further investigation needed
It tells you the exact dollar cost of the incident
It automatically fixes the underlying problem
questions.explain: That gap is deliberate — Azure Monitor's job is fast, cheap notification that something needs attention; finding out why is what DMVs and Extended Events are for.

questions.q: Why does a baseline (from Lesson 38) matter when setting alert thresholds?
options: The same raw percentage means something different depending on what's normal for that specific database — 80% DTU is alarming on a database that normally runs at 40%, but expected on one that normally runs at 75%
Baselines have no relationship to alert thresholds at all
Alert thresholds must always be set to exactly 50% regardless of baseline
Baselines are only used for storage metrics, never for CPU or DTU
questions.explain: The baseline gives the raw metric context, which is exactly what makes a well-chosen alert threshold meaningful instead of arbitrary.
